Ultimately from Latin -ānus.
Borrowed from Latin -ātus.

parole.significato: Suffix used to form agent nouns (both animate and inanimate) from verbs in -увати (-uvaty) and -ова́ти (-ováty): -ator,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ātor, from -tor added to verbs in -āre. Influenced by French -ateur, itself a borrowing from the same Latin suffix.
From Latin -ātiō, an alternative form of -tiō. Parsable as -а (-a) + -ція (-cija).

parole.significato: Suffix appended to adjective-, noun- and verb-stem roots to create nouns
parole.testo: Unknown. Perhaps from Latin -ērium, probably, irregularly via the poorly attested earlier *-yrъ. Compare Czech -ýř, Proto-Slavic *-(t)yrь, Russian -ы́рь (-ýrʹ).

From Latin -issa, borrowed from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa), from -ῐᾰ (-ĭă), from Proto-Indo-European *-ih₂, from *-is (i-stem suffix) + *-h₂ (neuter plural suffix). In turn borrowed from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa).
From Latin -ficātiō. Reanalyzed as -ифік (-yfik) + -а́ція (-ácija).

Borrowed from Latin audientia.

parole.significato: Independent research, observation of something (as opposed to second hand accounts)
parole.testo: From New Latin autopsia, from Ancient Greek αὐτοψῐ́ᾱ (autopsĭ́ā, “seeing with one's own eyes”).

parole.significato: to authorize (grant approval or permission for, especially the distribution or reproduction of texts)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre. Compare Russian авторизова́ть (avtorizovátʹ), Polish autoryzować.

parole.significato: agglomeration (the act or process of collecting in a mass; a heaping together)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin agglomerātiō. Compare Russian агломера́ция (aglomerácija), Belarusian агламера́цыя (ahlamjerácyja), Polish aglomeracja.

parole.significato: aggressor (the person or country that first attacks or makes an aggression)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin aggressor, from aggredior.

parole.significato: adaptation (process of adapting something or becoming adapted to a situation)
parole.testo: Derived via Western European languages from Medieval Latin adaptātiō, from Latin adaptō. Compare Russian адапта́ция (adaptácija), Belarusian адапта́цыя (adaptácyja), Polish adaptacja. By surface analysis, адапт- (adapt-) + -ація (-acija)
Calque of Latin advocatus diaboli. Compare Russian адвока́т дья́вола (advokát dʹjávola).

From Latin administrō, with -ува́ти (-uváty) ending. Compare Russian администри́ровать (administrírovatʹ), Belarusian адміністрава́ць (administravácʹ), Polish administrować.

Borrowed from Latin accūsātīvus.
Borrowed from Latin accumulātiō.

parole.significato: share (financial instrument certifying part-ownership of a company)
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Latin āctiō. Compare Russian а́кция (ákcija), Belarusian а́кцыя (ákcyja), Polish akcja.
From Medieval Latin algorismus, from Arabic الخَوَارِزْمِيّ (al-ḵawārizmiyy), the nisba of Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi.
Borrowed from Latin althaea.

parole.significato: alphabet (an ordered set of letters used in a language), especially the Latin alphabet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alphabētum (“alphabet”), from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha, “alpha”) and βήτα (bḗta, “beta”) (the names of the first two letters in the Greek alphabet). From Latin analyticus, from Ancient Greek ἀναλυτικός (analutikós). Compare Russian анали́тик (analítik), Polish analityk.

From Latin anatomia, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “dissection”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, incise”). Compare Russian анато́мия (anatómija), Polish anatomia.

Borrowed from Latin anīsum.

parole.significato: to applaud, to clap (express approval by clapping the hands)
parole.testo: From French applaudir + -ува́ти (-uváty), from Latin applaudō. Compare Russian аплоди́ровать (aplodírovatʹ), Belarusian апладзі́раваць (apladzíravacʹ).
Borrowed from Latin approbātiō.

parole.significato: Arachis (genus within the family Fabaceae – flowering plants, of which the peanut is the best known)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin arachis, from Ancient Greek (see ἄρακος (árakos), ἀράχιδνα (arákhidna)). Compare Russian ара́хис (aráxis).

parole.significato: argument (fact or statement used to support a proposition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin argumentum.

parole.significato: area (of distribution/dispersion of inhabitants belonging to an ethnos, tribe, language community, etc.)

parole.significato: articulation (the manner in which a phoneme is pronounced)
parole.testo: From Latin articulātiō. Compare Russian артикуля́ция (artikuljácija), Belarusian артыкуля́цыя (artykuljácyja), Polish artykulacja.
Ultimately from Latin architectūra, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn). Cognate with Russian архитекту́ра (arxitektúra), Belarusian архітэкту́ра (arxitektúra), Polish architektura.
Borrowed from Latin assignātiō.

parole.significato: to assimilate (to absorb (a person or people) into a community or culture)
parole.testo: From асиміл(я́ція) (asymil(jácija)) + -юва́ти (-juváty), ultimately from Latin assimulō. Compare Russian ассимили́ровать (assimilírovatʹ), Belarusian асімілява́ць (asimiljavácʹ), Polish asymilować.

Ultimately derived from Latin audītōrium. Compare Russian аудито́рия (auditórija), Polish audytorium.

parole.significato: vacuum (region of space that contains no matter)

parole.significato: to taste, to degust, to degustate (to sample the flavour of something orally)

parole.significato: dissident (person who formally opposes the current political structure)

parole.significato: to discuss, to debate (about something: про (pro) + accusative)

parole.significato: distillate (the liquid that has been condensed from vapour during distillation)
